title: Key West, Florida Travel Guide

hero.alt: Key West waterfront, historic Old Town, and tropical Florida Keys
hero.headline: Key West, Florida Travel Guide
hero.subheadline: Plan Key West around historic Old Town, sunset waterfronts, snorkeling and sailing, island culture, and remote Dry Tortugas adventures.

overview: Key West is an island city at the end of the Overseas Highway, where historic neighborhoods, maritime culture, tropical architecture, and water-based recreation are packed into a remarkably small area. Old Town is compact enough to explore on foot or bike, while the Historic Seaport, Mallory Square, and working waterfront make the surrounding water part of everyday visitor life.

The best itineraries balance land and sea. Spend time in Old Town and its museums, then reserve at least one block for sailing, snorkeling, kayaking, fishing, or an eco-tour. Dry Tortugas National Park is a separate remote national park about 70 miles west of Key West and requires its own transportation and planning; it should never be treated as a neighborhood or ordinary city attraction.

highlights.title: Historic Old Town
highlights.description: Walk among wooden Conch houses, museums, shaded side streets, Bahama Village, and the commercial energy of Duval Street.

highlights.title: Sunset and waterfront life
highlights.description: Mallory Square, the Historic Seaport, and harbor cruises turn the edge of the island into one of Key West's defining experiences.

highlights.title: Water adventures
highlights.description: Snorkeling, sailing, kayaking, fishing, sandbar trips, and eco-tours reveal the shallow-water and marine landscapes surrounding the island.

highlights.title: Gateway to Dry Tortugas
highlights.description: Ferry and seaplane departures from Key West provide access to remote Garden Key and Fort Jefferson in a separate National Park Service unit.

thingsToDo.title: Walk through Historic Old Town
thingsToDo.description: Old Town is the best place to understand Key West beyond its waterfront bars and excursion boats. Walk or bike the side streets around Whitehead, Caroline, Fleming, and neighboring blocks to see wooden cottages, larger historic homes, tropical gardens, churches, museums, and the architecture shaped by Bahamian and maritime influences. Duval Street is part of the experience, but the quieter streets reveal more of the island's character. Start in the morning before heat and crowds build, then use museums or shaded stops during the middle of the day.

thingsToDo.title: See sunset at Mallory Square
thingsToDo.description: Mallory Square is Key West's traditional sunset gathering place, where performers, vendors, visitors, boats, and the waterfront come together at the western edge of Old Town. Arrive before sunset so the experience is more than a last-minute photograph, then continue on foot into nearby streets or the Historic Seaport. Sunset conditions vary with clouds and weather, so treat the gathering itself as the attraction rather than requiring a perfect horizon view.

thingsToDo.title: Explore the Historic Seaport
thingsToDo.description: The Historic Seaport is both a visitor district and a working departure point for boats. Walk the harbor to see charter vessels, schooners, fishing boats, restaurants, and waterfront activity, then use it as the starting point for a sailing, snorkeling, fishing, or eco-tour. This is a better way to understand Key West's maritime identity than treating individual boat brands or operators as attractions. Morning departures suit active water trips, while late afternoon and evening work well for harbor walks and sunset cruises.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Fort Zachary Taylor Historic State Park
thingsToDo.description: Fort Zachary Taylor Historic State Park combines a beach with a nineteenth-century coastal fort at the southwest edge of Key West. It is a strong half-day choice when you want swimming or snorkeling without giving up historical context. The shoreline is different from the broad sandy beaches many travelers expect elsewhere in Florida, so water shoes can be useful. Check state-park conditions, hours, and any water advisories before visiting, and allow time to explore the fort rather than using the site only as a beach stop.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Hemingway Home and literary Key West
thingsToDo.description: Ernest Hemingway lived in Key West during the 1930s, and his former Whitehead Street home provides a tangible link to the island's long literary reputation. The house works best as part of a broader Old Town walk rather than as an isolated celebrity stop. Nearby streets also connect to other writers, artists, and architectural history that helped turn Key West into a distinctive cultural destination. Check current tour arrangements and admission details before visiting.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Harry S. Truman Little White House
thingsToDo.description: The Truman Little White House adds an important twentieth-century political chapter to Key West. President Harry S. Truman used the former naval officers' residence repeatedly during his presidency, and the museum interprets those stays within the larger history of the naval station and island. It fits naturally with a walk through the Truman Annex and western Old Town and provides an indoor cultural stop during the hottest part of the day.

thingsToDo.title: Get on the water
thingsToDo.description: Key West makes the most sense when at least part of the trip happens off land. Snorkeling trips, sailing, kayaking, fishing charters, wildlife-focused eco-tours, and sandbar outings all reveal the shallow marine environment surrounding the lower Florida Keys. Choose the experience by interest and conditions rather than by boat model or operator name. Wind, visibility, tides, and thunderstorms can affect the day, so keep some flexibility and follow the captain's weather guidance.

thingsToDo.title: Plan a Dry Tortugas National Park day trip
thingsToDo.description: Dry Tortugas National Park is a remote federal park about 70 miles west of Key West with no road access. Ferry and seaplane visitors travel from Key West to Garden Key, home to Fort Jefferson, swimming and snorkeling areas, and the park's main visitor facilities. Transportation is limited and often requires advance reservations, so this should be planned as a dedicated excursion rather than added casually to another day. Bring what the operator and National Park Service recommend, review current conditions, and remember that the Dry Tortugas are a separate national park, not part of the City of Key West.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Winter and spring are popular; summer and fall require weather flexibility
bullets: Winter through spring generally brings milder temperatures and strong demand, so lodging and popular boat trips can book well ahead.
Summer is hot and humid, with frequent sun exposure and the potential for afternoon thunderstorms; plan active land sightseeing early and stay flexible on the water.
Atlantic hurricane season runs from June through November. Travelers in that period should monitor forecasts and understand cancellation and evacuation policies.
Water visibility, wind, sea state, and wildlife conditions vary throughout the year, so no single month guarantees ideal snorkeling, sailing, or fishing conditions.

travelTips: Walk or bike Old Town when practical; short distances can make moving and parking a car more trouble than it is worth.
Use sun protection and carry water even on casual sightseeing days; heat and humidity can make a compact island feel less walkable at midday.
Book high-demand sailing, snorkeling, fishing, sunset, and Dry Tortugas transportation in advance when your dates are fixed.
Keep weather flexibility in any water-based itinerary, especially during summer and hurricane season.
Distinguish Key West from the rest of the Florida Keys and from Dry Tortugas National Park; nearby islands, reefs, and protected areas have different access rules and jurisdictions.

faq.q: How many days are ideal for Key West?
faq.a: Three days is enough for Old Town, the waterfront, and one substantial water experience. Four days is better if you want a Dry Tortugas trip without sacrificing a relaxed island day.

faq.q: Do I need a car in Key West?
faq.a: Not for most Old Town itineraries. Walking, biking, public transportation, trolleys, taxis, and rideshare can cover the compact central area. A car is more useful when Key West is part of a longer Florida Keys road trip.

faq.q: Is Dry Tortugas National Park in Key West?
faq.a: No. It is a separate National Park Service unit about 70 miles west of Key West. There are no roads to the park; visitors reach it by ferry, seaplane, private boat, or permitted charter.

faq.q: Is Key West mainly a beach destination?
faq.a: No. Beaches are part of the trip, but Key West is equally defined by Old Town history, architecture, maritime culture, museums, sailing, snorkeling, fishing, and sunset waterfront life.

faq.q: Should I book water tours in advance?
faq.a: Yes for popular departures and busy travel periods. Keep enough flexibility to accommodate weather changes, since wind and sea conditions can alter or cancel water activities.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Key West is a small island city at the western end of the inhabited Florida Keys. Its identity comes from the intersection of maritime work, Caribbean and Bahamian influences, Cuban connections, military history, tourism, literature, and a built environment adapted to a hot coastal climate.

sections.heading: Geography & setting
paragraphs: The city occupies Key West and adjacent developed areas near the end of the Overseas Highway, surrounded by shallow subtropical waters. The island's limited land area explains why the waterfront, Old Town, neighborhoods, and visitor districts sit so close together. Reefs, channels, mangrove environments, and other Keys islands extend far beyond the city itself and should be treated as regional marine landscapes rather than municipal attractions.

sections.heading: History and culture
paragraphs: Key West's history includes Indigenous use of the Keys, Spanish and British colonial eras, wrecking and salvage, fishing and sponging, Cuban cigar making, Bahamian migration, U.S. naval activity, and twentieth-century tourism. Bahama Village, Conch architecture, literary landmarks, historic churches, museums, and the working seaport preserve different parts of that story.

sections.heading: Water and outdoor life
paragraphs: Boating is not an optional side note in Key West; it is one of the main ways to understand the destination. Sailing, snorkeling, fishing, paddling, wildlife trips, and sandbar excursions connect visitors to the surrounding marine environment. Dry Tortugas National Park extends that experience into a remote island park but remains a separate federal destination requiring advance planning.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: Old Town is compact and often easiest to explore on foot or bicycle. Trolleys, buses, taxis, pedi-cabs, and rideshare provide alternatives when heat or distance becomes uncomfortable. Parking can be limited and expensive in the most visited areas, so travelers staying centrally often gain little from moving a car for short trips.
